claims.text: Laser cladding a Ni-W-B alloy onto a damaged surface can produce an in situ graded layer.
The laser-clad Ni-W-B layer will be crack resistant.
The laser-clad surface will improve wear, corrosion, and high-temperature performance relative to traditional fusion-welding repairs and untreated surfaces.
The target component microstructure is prone to hot cracking during conventional fusion welding.
Controlled laser energy density and an inert atmosphere will provide rapid melting and solidification.
The proposed clad surface is intended for aggressive corrosive environments and service temperatures up to approximately 600°C.
Laser cladding will create a refined, compositionally or structurally graded microstructure.
The clad microstructure will contain in situ formed tungsten borides embedded in a martensitic matrix.
The graded microstructure will create a continuous gradient in hardness and toughness.
The hardness and toughness gradient will resist crack initiation.
Rapid melting and resolidification during laser cladding will promote fine reinforcing phases such as tungsten borides.
Fine tungsten-boride reinforcing phases will increase hardness and inhibit grain growth.
The refined microstructure will reduce susceptibility to hot cracking.
The refined microstructure will improve wear and corrosion resistance.
The clad surface will provide at least a 20% improvement in hardness relative to both fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The clad surface will provide at least a 20% improvement in wear resistance relative to both fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The clad surface will exhibit significantly fewer hot-cracking incidents than fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
Successful performance depends on optimization of laser parameters, powder composition, and cladding geometry.
Service temperatures above 600°C may limit performance.
Complex component geometries that prevent uniform cladding may limit successful implementation.
